statement: Kim has 16 minutes left and six unread 5-point questions. Two would take her 5 minutes to solve and four would take 12 minutes. Reading a question takes 1 minute and shows which kind it is. Every question she finishes is right. How many points can she be sure of, whatever order the questions are in?

choices.misconception: I thought she cannot be sure of anything, because she does not know where the quick questions are.
I had her read all six questions first, 6 minutes, and then counted another minute to read each quick one again, so in the 10 minutes left only one 1 + 5 = 6 minute question fits.
I fitted three 5-minute questions into 16 minutes, forgetting that only two of the questions are quick.
I counted all six questions, as if her guesses on the unfinished ones would all be right.

hints: Where could the two quick questions be, in the worst case?
Plan for the worst case. Reading costs only 1 minute but a long question costs 12. Reading until she finds a quick one, solving it, and then reading on wastes the least time.
Worst case: the quick ones are the last two she reads. Reading all six takes 6 minutes and solving the two quick ones takes 10 more, exactly 16.

solutions.reliable: Strategy: read questions one at a time; skip each long one, and solve each quick one as soon as it is found. However the questions are ordered, she spends at most 6 minutes reading and 5 + 5 = 10 minutes solving, a total of 16, so she always finishes both quick ones: 10 points for sure. She cannot be sure of more: finishing a third question means solving a long one, and 1 + 12 for it plus 1 + 5 + 1 + 5 for the two quick ones is 25 minutes, far more than 16. The transferable idea: in the 5-point block, a minute spent reading every question before committing is cheap, and committing blindly to the first one can cost the whole block.

whyOnTest: The 5-point block rewards reading everything before committing; this puts numbers on why working blindly in order can cost points.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
